newsitem.title: UK: LME drifts at mid-session, business is light.
newsitem.headline: LME drifts at mid-session, business is light.

text.p: Base metal markets turned back after a steady start during slow Thursday LME ring trading, with overhead reluctance seen in all contracts, traders said.
"It has been very slow all morning. Europe is closed for May Day, the Japanese are also out," one trader said.

Copper led the way, and after failing to sustain any sort of challenge above $2,380 and follow through to Wednesday's smart rally, prices gradually turned turtle. A slightly softer tone in the spreads also undermined sentiment, traders said.

Stocks rose by 2,000 tonnes, the second successive daily increase, but there were nevertheless positive signs from the data. The various tonnages delivered into European warehouses were attracted by the recent high backwardation, and could easily move back out.
Similar considerations applied to the metal moving into Comex, which is likely to revert to US market warehouses when the arbitrage re-adjusts, some traders said.
Also, there was 2,150 tonnes taken out of Singapore, and further falls in the 14,050 tonnes of LME copper there are likely in coming weeks, they said.
Fundamentals remain in place, with workers at Chile's 75,000-tonne Quebrada Blanca mine striking on Wednesday. There is a partial stoppage at Escondida.
Three months prices concluded the kerb at $2,372 a tonne, a $7 loss from Wednesday after losing grips with $2,375/80 under some cash pricing sales. The cash/threes backwardation was trading at $80.

Aluminium initially pushed up towards a $1,650 objective, attempting to build on a constructive chart picture and another fall in inventories. But by the rings prices were on the retreat, with some profit-taking witnessed, and final morning trade was at $1,629, a $16 loss.

The alloy market was initially helped by a 1,040-tonne stock fall, which was believed to represent material moving from Europe to the Far East. Business was at a high $1,520 on the pre-market, but the general softness of the complex resulted in prices being marked lower. Three months was at $1,500/05 at the end of the kerb, against a previous $1,515.
Zinc drifted back in slow conditions, and was last at $1,271, down $2. Lead continued to correct from 18-month lows hit earlier this week, closing $4 steadier at $628.

Tin fluctuated narrowly either side of Wednesday's close of $5,700, with last trade at $5,705. Nickel crumbled under liquidation, and was $50 softer at $7,330. Stock movements in both these markets were minimal.
